title: When Should You Accelerate Your Child?
author: Chad Aldeman
summary: Chad Aldeman examines Fairfax County Public Schools' automatic-enrollment policy for algebra acceleration, which projects 84.5% of 8th graders in Algebra I or higher by next year -- far above national averages. Using Virginia SOL end-of-course exam data, he shows that pass rates are high across accelerated cohorts: 91.9% for 8th-grade Algebra I takers, 98.9% for 7th-graders, and 100% for 6th-graders. Aldeman invites guest commenter Pamela Hobart to explain why automatic opt-out enrollment policies are superior to recommendation-based systems: subjective gating leaves too much room for teacher bias and anti-acceleration defaults, particularly harming girls and students of color. Research cited by Hobart finds that students who don't take Algebra 1 by 8th grade rarely catch up -- top scorers who took it as 8th-graders were 3x to 55x more likely to pursue chemistry and physics than equally capable peers who waited. Aldeman's verdict: Fairfax is doing something clearly right, but the district's opt-out letter subtly undermines the policy by framing acceleration as a risk rather than an opportunity.
points: * Fairfax County projects 84.5% of 8th graders in Algebra I or higher by next school year, with Virginia's statewide end-of-course exams providing an accountability backstop on quality. * Pass rates strongly suggest districts are underaccelerating: 91.9% of 8th-grade Algebra takers passed, 98.9% of 7th-graders, and 100% of 6th-graders -- with almost certainly some selection effects. * Automatic opt-out policies remove teacher anti-acceleration bias; subjective recommendation systems rarely self-correct because it's more noticeable when a student is moved up than quietly kept behind. * Students who don't take Algebra 1 by 8th grade rarely catch up: top scorers accelerated to 8th-grade algebra were 3x to 55x more likely to take chemistry and physics than equally capable peers who waited. * Fairfax's opt-out letter subtly undermines the spirit of Virginia's HB2868 by framing the accelerated placement as a 'risky bet requiring sophisticated discernment' rather than earned opportunity.
quotes: These high pass rates suggest that districts across Virginia may be just a little too choosy about which students get access to advanced math classes.
Subjective acceleration choices, like those depending strictly on teacher recommendation, leave too much room for bias and unchecked discretion.
Automatic, opt-out acceleration policies can serve as an important check on school and teacher anti-acceleration biases.
The kids who don't take Algebra 1 by 8th grade rarely catch up (top scorers who took 8th-grade algebra were 3x to 55x more likely to take chemistry and physics than equally capable peers who waited).
If someone offered tutoring that promised a 3x to 55x enhanced chance of giving students a STEM career, parents would be lining up to buy it!
Instead of advertising the benefits of accelerated math, Fairfax County invites parents to focus on the risk to their students' GPA.
Kudos to Fairfax County (and Virginia state policymakers). They're clearly doing something right here, but they may still have some work to do to convince more parents that this is a good thing.
